blocks.content: The High Courts and the Supreme Court can order the CBI to investigate a crime anywhere in the country without the consent of the State.

rows: Blanket permission granted to CBI to conduct investigations against central employees in a state.
Case-by-case approval required from the state government for specific investigations.
CBI can seamlessly register cases and enter state jurisdiction without prior notice.
CBI must submit an application and wait for explicit approval before initiating action.
If withdrawn, CBI cannot register new cases without seeking specific consent.
Applies automatically to individual cases when general consent stands withdrawn.

items: CBI is NOT a statutory body; it is an executive body deriving investigative powers from the DSPE Act, 1946.
Withdrawal of general consent by a State does not affect ongoing investigations initiated prior to the withdrawal.
The CBI acts as the National Central Bureau (NCB) of Interpol in India.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The CBI derives its powers to investigate from the Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946.
CBI has jurisdiction to investigate offences primarily in Union Territories and against Central Government employees.
To extend its investigation into a State, consent of that State government is mandatory under Section 6 of the DSPE Act.
State consent can be either 'General Consent' (blanket permission) or 'Specific Consent' (case-by-case approval).
The Supreme Court and High Courts can direct the CBI to investigate a crime anywhere in the country without the consent of the State.
